newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Snacking can help you lose weight, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Snacking can help you lose weight, study finds.

text.p: Snacking can help slimmers lose weight but what you eat and when is paramount to success, British researchers told a conference on Friday.

Other research confirmed that both metabolism and what people eat combine to cause obesity -- and offered some hints at ways to overcome the hopeless cycle that causes many slimmers to gain back more weight than they lose after a diet.

Norma Crombie of Queen Margaret College in Edinburgh said her team of researchers had found that eating a snack 90 minutes before a meal gave the body enough time to absorb the food and reduce appetite. But a snack 30 minutes before mealtime did not cut appetite by as much and simply added calories, she said.

"Much greater compensation for the pre-meal snack occurred at dinner than at lunch," she told the Eighth European Conference on Obesity in Dublin, saying her group had expanded the study to check their results.
But what is eaten is as important as timing, found Jennie MacDiarmid of the University of Leeds.
She surveyed several hundred British men and women and found even those who seemed to watch what they ate occasionally binged on high-fat foods and probably laid down extra fat as a result.

One woman who normally avoided fat blew her careful diet in just one lunch by eating a series of small sandwiches loaded with fat. It added more than 100 grams of fat -- worth 900 calories -- to her day's intake.
"Clearly...high-fat consumers and even some typically low-fat consumers have the capacity to consume extremely large amounts of fat," MacDiarmid said.
John Cooling, a researcher at Leeds, found some people just don't seem to notice they are eating fatty foods. They tested young men aged 20 to 25 and fed them controlled meals.
"The high-fat eaters ate almost the same weight of food whether we gave them fat or carbohydrate," he said.
Fat has many more calories than protein or carbohydrate and so they ate many more calories -- sometimes up to 600 extra calories than normal in a meal -- without seeming to know it.
But the men with a normally lower fat diet, determined through careful interviews, ate to a certain level of calories and then stopped.
"The signals that bring about satiety seem to be stronger in low-fat consumers," Cooling said.
Reinhard Geldszus and colleagues at the Medizenschen Hochschule in Hanover, Germany found more evidence that the hormone leptin may be one of those indicators.
Animal tests have shown the hormone is strongly associated with body fat levels and that it may help regulate metabolism.

Geldszus's group tested leptin levels in 227 normal women and 149 obese women. The obese women started out with significantly higher leptin levels than the normal-weight women. All were then put on a very low-calorie, high-protein liquid diet.
"Leptin levels crashed in the obese group," Geldszus said. They went steadily down for three months and then levelled out.
It was possible, Geldszus said, that the high leptin levels were the body's attempt to deal with a high-fat diet or some other factor in the obese women's lives.
Or it could mean their bodies did not react properly to leptin, which scientists think is one signaller that tells the body it has had enough to eat.
Geldszus and other researchers said it might be possible to give leptin to dieters to help them control the lowered metabolism that follows a low-calorie diet.
This slow-down in energy has undermined many a weight-loss regimen and has led many experts to say that diets do not work.
